topicName: Action Recognition and Optical Flow in Video
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Action Recognition and Optical Flow in Video"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Video Understanding"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Video analysis extends computer vision from static spatial domains into the temporal dimension. Action recognition involves classifying what is happening in a video clip. Unlike image classification, video tasks require capturing both spatial appearance (objects, scenes) and temporal dynamics (movement, motion patterns over time)."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"The Role of Optical Flow"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"Optical flow is the pattern of apparent motion of image objects between two consecutive frames caused by the relative movement of the object or the camera. It computes a displacement vector field (u, v) for every pixel, representing movement from frame t to frame t+1."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Sparse Optical Flow (e.g., Lucas-Kanade): Calculates motion vectors for a sparse set of feature points (like corners)."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Dense Optical Flow (e.g., Farneback, FlowNet): Calculates motion vectors for every single pixel in the image frame."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Computing Dense Optical Flow using OpenCV"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Below is a Python implementation using OpenCV to compute and visualize dense optical flow between two consecutive video frames."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"import cv2
import numpy as np

# Load two consecutive frames in grayscale
frame1 = cv2.imread('frame1.jpg', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
frame2 = cv2.imread('frame2.jpg', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

# Compute dense optical flow using Farneback algorithm
flow = cv2.calcOpticalFlowFarneback(frame1, frame2, None, 0.5, 3, 15, 3, 5, 1.2, 0)

# Extract magnitude and angle of 2D motion vectors
magnitude, angle = cv2.cartToPolar(flow[..., 0], flow[..., 1])

# Create HSV representation for visualization
hsv = np.zeros((frame1.shape[0], frame1.shape[1], 3), dtype=np.uint8)
hsv[..., 1] = 255
hsv[..., 0] = angle * 180 / np.pi / 2
hsv[..., 2] = cv2.normalize(magnitude, None, 0, 255, cv2.NORM_MINMAX)

# Convert HSV to BGR for display
flow_bgr = cv2.cvtColor(hsv, cv2.COLOR_HSV2BGR)
cv2.imwrite('optical_flow_result.jpg', flow_bgr)"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Two-Stream Networks for Action Recognition"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditional architectures combined spatial streams (taking raw RGB frames to capture appearance) and temporal streams (taking stacked optical flow frames to capture motion). The final action prediction is typically obtained by late fusion of the softmax scores from both streams."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Modern 3D Convolutional Networks (3D CNNs)"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern architectures such as I3D (Inflated 3D ConvNet) and SlowFast replace 2D spatial convolutions with 3D kernels (HxWxCXT). These models simultaneously learn spatial and temporal features directly from RGB video frames, reducing the reliance on pre-computed optical flow while maintaining high accuracy."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Action recognition requires understanding both appearance and motion. While optical flow provides explicit, robust motion cues that benefit deep learning models, modern 3D architectures offer end-to-end learning capabilities that continue to push the boundaries of automated video understanding."}]
